title: Vaulted firmware / signed updates discovery - Greyhaven Labs
next_steps: Redwood to send sealed-airgap security whitepaper and signed-binaries workflow doc
Customer to share on-prem BOM and maintenance blackout windows
Schedule 2-hr bench run in Greyhaven test lab week of 2027-10-11
Follow-up call to review signed update process with SRE and security (w/ Priya)
action_items: Alex Martinez: email airgap update playbook + link to SOC2/ISO pack - due 2027-10-01
Aaron Lee: export rack/u-plug BOM and patch window spreadsheet - due 2027-10-04
Priya Desai: prepare test-plan for offline benchmark run (includes 5k token synth load) - due 2027-10-08
Keisha Monroe: list compliance questions and internal approval timeline - due 2027-10-05
summary: Discovery call about deploying Redwood in a fully isolated Greyhaven facility. Primary focus: offline update process, signed firmware/artifact workflow, hardware constraints (embedded GPUs, rack power), and compliance sign-offs. Team wants clear rollback and audit trail, prefer signed binaries via HSM/KMS path, and minimal internet touchpoints.
topics: bench testing plan and pilot scope
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martinez (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to learn about Greyhaven's constraints and walk through our offline update story. 
[00:18] Dr. Mira Patel (Greyhaven CTO): Thanks Alex. We run a heavily regulated path lab environment, zero internet outbound from inference nodes. So main question: how do you push model updates, security patches, and critical hotfixes without opening a hole?
[00:33] Sanjay Rao (Redwood SE): Totally, Mira. Our on-prem package supports a sealed deployment model. Updates can be delivered as signed bundles — we provide a signing tool, or you can sign with your HSM. We also have a checksum verification at runtime and an audit log.
[00:48] Aaron Lee (Greyhaven Infra): When you say "signing tool" — is that the Redwood CA? We need private key control inside our FIPS HSM. We cannot hand over keys.
[00:58] Priya Desai (Redwood SE): Correct, you keep keys. The flow we usually recommend: Redwood generates release artifacts, you validate and then re-sign with your HSM; the nodes validate signatures against a local trust store. We also support signed timestamps so you have non-repudiation for updates.
[01:15] Keisha Monroe (Compliance): Do you produce a manifest that ties binaries to checksums and the included model hash? We need a verifiable chain for audit.
[01:25] Sanjay: Yes, manifest + provenance metadata. Small caveat: the auto-generated metadata sometimes has internal names ('redwood-infer-v2') that might not map to customer's naming. That's easy to map out in the release step.
[01:40] Tom Alvarez (Embedded Systems): On hardware, our nodes are small 1U appliances with Max-Q style GPUs (we call them T4L-something). We need exact supported GPU list and the binary size for model runtime so we can confirm flash storage fits.
[01:55] Alex: Understood. We can provide a BOM and per-model footprint matrix. Typical runtime for our quantized open models ranges 4-12GB on disk, but we can produce smaller quantized builds for constrained devices.
[02:12] Aaron: Also concerned about DRAC and physical access. In the sealed facility only authorized USBs can be used — can we ship updates on physical media?
[02:22] Priya: Yes, physical media is part of our offline update flow. We support signed USB image with a preflight verifier that checks signatures and manifest before applying. The process emits an immutable audit record.
[02:35] Keisha: For compliance we need to know who triggered the update in our SSO. Is there a way to capture the initiating identity even when the node is offline?
[02:45] Sanjay: We recommend an 'update request token' that is minted while connected in the control plane, then printed as a QR/PK into the signed bundle. When you re-sign in your HSM, that token and the re-signer identity are recorded in the bundle metadata. Upon apply, the node logs the token and the local admin principal.
[03:05] Dr. Mira: Sounds plausible, but any change window needs to be short. Our lab has 1-hour nightly windows.
[03:12] Alex: Noted. We'll verify patch time for hotfix vs full model swap. We also have differential update capability for KV/cached weights so a lot of updates are smaller.
[03:23] Tom: Differential updates sound good, but how do you handle KV cache invalidation?
[03:28] Sanjay: The runtime keeps a prefix cache; the update API can specify a cache sweep or a warm-start option. For total safety in hermetic environments, we recommend a cold restart after model swap during the maintenance window.
[03:42] Aaron: Benchmarks — can you run a simulated 5k token per-request workload? We care about 99th percentile latency and sustained throughput.
[03:50] Priya: Absolutely. For the pilot we'll propose a 2-hour stress run with synthetic traces. We'll instrument per-token latency, batch sizes, and memory pressure.
[04:02] Keisha: Audit and logging retention — we need immutable logs for 7 years for certain experiments. Do you support storing logs locally or exporting to our SIEM via a pull model?
[04:12] Sanjay: We have an append-only local audit ledger and a pull-based exporter that can be run from within your network to push to your SIEM or long-term store. We also emit an export artifact you can checksum and archive on removable media.
[04:28] Dr. Mira: Who from Redwood will be our day-of contact during the pilot? We want an SE onsite or remote standby.
[04:36] Alex: Priya will be the primary SE for the pilot and I'm the AE managing the engagement. We'll include two on-call SREs for the bench run.
[04:44] Aaron: A note on hardware: our power budget per rack is tight — 12kW per rack is the max. Do you have per-node power specs?
[04:54] Priya: We'll share a power/perf matrix. Also for GPUs we provide supported driver bundles. For offline installs, you'd load driver packages as part of the signed bundle.
[05:05] Tom: Do you support custom kernel modules? Our telemetry requires an in-house module for NIC telemetry.
[05:12] Sanjay: We can include prebuilt kernel modules in the artifact, but signing them and allowing them to load depends on your secure boot policy. We have guidance for integrating with secure boot and signed kernel modules.
[05:25] Keisha: Regarding identity: we have an internal SSO (SAML) and we want RBAC aligned to AD groups. How does Redwood map tokens to groups offline?
[05:35] Alex: We support a bootstrap where you provide a user-to-role mapping in a sealed config bundle. The tokens are short-lived and can be minted on a jump host and embedded in the update artifact if needed.
[05:46] Dr. Mira: Let's talk about upgrade rollback. If a model swap causes a regression, what's the fastest rollback?
[05:52] Priya: The node keeps the previous model snapshot and can revert within a few minutes, but it depends on model size and whether you need to cold restart. We recommend keeping at least one previous snapshot on disk for fast rollback.
[06:06] Aaron: For very constrained flash storage, do you stream models from a nearby NFS in the sealed network?
[06:13] Sanjay: Yes, the runtime supports local NFS or object store inside your network. Streaming reduces disk use but increases startup latency. That's a tradeoff we can tune.
[06:25] Keisha: Encryption at rest: are keys stored in node TPMs or do you require HSM?
[06:31] Alex: We support both. You can use TPM-bound keys for node-local encryption and HSM for signing and central key custody.
[06:38] Tom: Any concerns about quantization accuracy when you do smaller builds? We train our own models and need to preserve accuracy thresholds.
[06:45] Priya: We do model quantization profiles with shadow runs to compare outputs. For critical clinical models we recommend a regression test suite with your prompts. We'll help set thresholds and monitoring.
[06:58] Dr. Mira: Monitoring — since nodes are offline, how will Redwood alert on model regressions?
[07:04] Sanjay: You can run local evals against golden prompt sets. The node will emit evaluation reports that you can pull out and ship to your analytics cluster. We can also set up offline telemetry collectors that you run during maintenance windows.
[07:17] Aaron: Let's address procurement: do you ship signed installers with a digest we can verify in our supply chain tool?
[07:24] Alex: Yes, we include signed digests and a reproducible build artifact. You can validate signatures against keys in your trust store.
[07:31] Keisha: Any special SOC2 or ISO attachments for on-prem? The security pack we saw was generic.
[07:36] Priya: We'll send a tailored security Annex for air-gapped deployments — includes HSM patterns, offline update guide, and audit log examples. We'll also include our SOC2 attestations and a summary tailored to Greyhaven constraints.
[07:50] Dr. Mira: Timeline — goal is pilot before Q4 2027, ideally November.
[07:56] Alex: Sounds doable. We'll align resources.
[08:00] Tom: A couple quick technical clarifications: 1) what's your preferred physical media image format? 2) Do you support TPM-based measured boot attestation?
[08:08] Priya: 1) We typically use an ISO/IMG that you dd to a signed USB. 2) Yes, we integrate with TPM attestation for measured boot and will provide a reference verifier.
[08:18] Aaron: Any idea on rollback SLOs? We need a documented RTO and RPO for each update class.
[08:25] Sanjay: We'll supply an update-class SLO table: critical hotfix (RTO < 30 minutes), model swap (RTO depends on size, typical < 45 minutes with preloaded snapshot), full OS patch (may require a longer window and physical reboot).
[08:42] Keisha: For legal we need a chain-of-custody for the physical media, receipts and signatures. Can you support an asset transfer form?
[08:50] Alex: Yes, we can provide a chain-of-custody template and logging that ties to the signed artifact.
[08:59] Dr. Mira: For the pilot scope we'd like to test two models: a small diagnostic classifier and a medium-sized conversational assistant. We'll define acceptance criteria (latency, output drift).
[09:12] Priya: Great. We'll include regression harness and evaluation metrics.
[09:18] Aaron: One more: how do you handle license updates for upstream open models? Offline environments sometimes need license reconciliation.
[09:26] Sanjay: We include license manifests for models and can provide a legal export package listing versions and license texts.
[09:34] Tom: Any required kernel patches? Our appliance runs a locked kernel.
[09:38] Priya: We try to avoid kernel-level changes; most runtime requires standard userland libs and drivers. We'll produce driver bundles you can vet.
[09:47] Keisha: Security question: can the audit log be write-once? We use WORM storage for some artifacts.
[09:53] Sanjay: Exported audit artifacts are compatible with WORM storage; locally we provide append-only ledger semantics.
[10:01] Alex: Okay let's move toward next steps — we'll email the security annex and the offline update playbook, and propose pilot dates.
[10:09] Dr. Mira: Sounds good. Any blockers from your side?
[10:13] Priya: We'll need your BOM and maintenance windows to finalize the pilot plan.
[10:18] Aaron: We'll compile that this week.
[10:22] Keisha: Also expecting an internal compliance questionnaire — we'll share it.
[10:26] Alex: Great. We'll reconvene after we exchange docs.
[10:30] [-- 00:10:30 to 00:30:00 redacted for internal Q/A; participants went into technical minutiae --]
[30:01] Tom: Back to the group — quick note on network topology: all nodes are on an isolated VLAN with one jump-host that has limited egress. The jump-host is where we intend to stage the signed bundles.
[30:12] Priya: That fits our pattern. We support a 'staging' flow where the jump-host validates signatures and then pushes to the node via the air-gapped provisioning channel. It's auditable.
[30:24] Aaron: How do you ensure integrity if the jump-host gets compromised?
[30:29] Sanjay: Defense-in-depth: the nodes verify signatures with a hardware-rooted trust store; even if the jump-host is compromised, you need the private signing keys to create a valid update.
[30:40] Keisha: On personnel: do you require onsite Redwood staff for initial install? We prefer remote installs with our engineers.
[30:46] Alex: We can do either. For this pilot we'll offer remote guided install plus an optional onsite day for handover if you want.
[30:55] Dr. Mira: Cost question — sealed deployments feel like enterprise licensing. What does pricing look like for private deployments?
[31:02] Alex: Pricing typically includes a platform fee for Private plus per-node runtime licenses; dedicated capacity and hosted differ. We'll send a tailored estimate after we scope node counts and support SLAs.
[31:14] Aaron: Any references for similar deployments? We prefer a pharma customer example.
[31:20] Priya: We can share an anonymized case study for a clinical diagnostics customer who ran an identical sealed flow. We'll strip PII.
[31:28] Keisha: Good. We also need to confirm breach disclosure timelines in the contract.
[31:34] Alex: Understood — we'll include standard incident SLA terms in the enterprise proposal.
[31:40] [-- participants discuss internal question ordering --]
[40:00] Sanjay: Quick technical note: when you re-sign artifacts with your HSM, we support two signature schemes — RSA-4096 and ECDSA-P384. Which do you prefer?
[40:10] Aaron: ECDSA-P384 is our standard.
[40:14] Priya: We'll configure reference keys for that.
[40:18] Tom: For the bench run, can you simulate a degraded I/O scenario to see behavior under flash pressure?
[40:24] Priya: Yes, we'll add a throttled I/O profile to the stress harness.
[40:30] Dr. Mira: Any known limitations for models >10B in air-gapped installs?
[40:36] Sanjay: Models that large require more RAM and potentially multiple-node sharding. For hermetic installs with constrained hardware we typically recommend distilled or quantized variants. We'll detail tradeoffs in the model catalog export.
[40:49] Aaron: Good. Also, please include any recommended kernel tunables for heavy batching.
[40:55] Priya: We'll provide a sysctl and cgroup tuning guide for low-latency inference.
[41:03] Keisha: Final governance note: we need a periodic attestation report from Redwood for the binary signing environment. Can you commit to quarterly attestations?
[41:11] Alex: We can include attestation artifacts and timeline in the contract.
[41:16] Dr. Mira: Great. Let's capture the next-step items.
[41:22] Alex: Recap: Redwood sends security annex + offline update playbook + per-model footprint and power matrix. Greyhaven to send BOM, blackout windows, compliance questionnaire, and a list of pilot models and test prompts. We'll schedule bench run wk of Oct 11.
[41:38] Keisha: Yep.
[41:40] Aaron: I'll coordinate the lab calendar.
[41:44] Priya: I'll draft the test plan and ping on the exact tooling.
[41:49] Tom: We'll circulate the hardware list.
[41:53] Dr. Mira: Thanks, everyone. Looking forward to the pilot.
[41:58] Alex: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email with links.
[42:03] [END 00:42:03] Note: some segments redacted for internal technical chatter; full internal transcript available on request.
